identification.summary: APT20 is a China-linked cyber espionage actor. Fox-IT (NCC Group) published Operation Wocao in December 2019, assessing with high confidence that the actor behind that activity is a Chinese group likely supporting Chinese government interests, and with medium confidence that its tools, techniques and procedures are those industry partners call APT20 [S2]. Earlier, in September 2014, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 attributed a series of watering-hole attacks using Poison Ivy to a group it called 'th3bug' [S1]. The imported record lists TH3Bug, Crawling Taurus (Unit 42) and VIOLIN PANDA (CrowdStrike) as APT20 aliases; those vendor mappings were not verified from a primary source.
identification.firstObserved: 2014-07 (earliest th3bug Poison Ivy sample Unit 42 saw, dated 14 July 2014) [S1]. MITRE dates Operation Wocao activity from December 2017 to December 2019 [S4].
identification.notes: Two distinct bodies of reporting are tied to the APT20 name: the 2014 th3bug watering holes (Unit 42) [S1] and the 2017-2019 Operation Wocao intrusions (Fox-IT) [S2][S4]. Fox-IT rates the Wocao-to-APT20 link only medium confidence, so facts from the two should not be merged without checking [S2]. Microsoft has no mapped name for APT20 in this encyclopedia record. Not a Microsoft-named cluster.

attribution.sponsor: Fox-IT judges the Operation Wocao actor to be a Chinese group likely working in support of Chinese government interests; this is Fox-IT's assessment, not a government attribution [S2][S6].
attribution.confidence: Fox-IT: high confidence in Chinese nationality and motive; medium confidence that the observed TTPs correspond to APT20 [S2]. Unit 42's 2014 report attributes the watering holes to the th3bug group based on shared Poison Ivy password and C2 infrastructure; the excerpts reviewed do not state a state-sponsor conclusion [S1].
attribution.basis: Fox-IT basis: the name Wocao comes from a Chinese expletive typed by an operator after losing access [S2][S6]. Unit 42 basis: Poison Ivy samples sharing a password and the same command-and-control server [S1].

objectives: Fox-IT assesses the Wocao actor is likely tasked with espionage supporting the interests of the Chinese government [S2]. The 2014 th3bug targeting of Uyghur sympathizers, a US university, a US computer maker office and an international telecom provider is consistent with intelligence collection, though Unit 42 excerpts reviewed do not state objectives [S1].

regions: Brazil, China, France, Germany, Italy, Mexico, Portugal, Spain, United Kingdom and United States (MITRE list for Operation Wocao) [S4]
targeting.notes: Fox-IT says victims were government entities, managed service providers and a wide variety of industries including energy, health care and high-tech [S2]. Press adds aviation, finance and insurance [S5]. The 2014 victims come from Unit 42 [S1].

capabilities.summary: 2014: compromise of legitimate websites as watering holes delivering Poison Ivy RAT variants; Unit 42 could not recover the initial exploit and said it was possibly the CVE-2014-0515 Adobe Flash exploit [S1]. 2017-2019 (Operation Wocao): initial access commonly through vulnerable web servers, often JBoss, sometimes already carrying web shells from other attackers; web shells for reconnaissance and lateral movement; credential dumping and capture of a password manager master password via keylogging; lateral tool transfer over SMB; deletion of tools and files to hide traces; and use of stolen VPN credentials as backdoors, in some cases despite two-factor authentication, which Fox-IT speculated was done with a stolen RSA SecurID software token [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: th3bug watering-hole attacks
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 (19 September 2014) reported that over the summer the group compromised several legitimate websites, including a well-known Uyghur-language site, and delivered Poison Ivy variants using the same C2. Victims included Uyghur sympathizers, an East Asian office of a major US computer maker, a major US university and an international telecom provider. Earliest sample dated 14 July 2014. Actors changed their Poison Ivy password, possibly after FireEye publicity [S1].

campaigns.name: Operation Wocao
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT named intrusions across more than 10 countries Operation Wocao. MITRE lists activity first seen December 2017 and last seen December 2019. Actors exploited web servers (often JBoss), used web shells, harvested credentials, moved laterally, bypassed 2FA on VPN accounts and deleted tools [S2][S4][S5].

campaigns.name: Public disclosure of Operation Wocao
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT published 'Operation Wocao: Shining a light on one of China's hidden hacking groups' dated 19 December 2019, rating the actor Chinese with high confidence and APT20 with medium confidence [S2][S6].

diamond.adversary: China-based group assessed by Fox-IT as working for Chinese government interests; linked to APT20 at medium confidence [S2].
diamond.capability: Poison Ivy RAT via watering holes (2014); web shells, JBoss exploitation, credential theft, SMB lateral movement, VPN and 2FA bypass, anti-forensic deletion (2017-2019) [S1][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites and shared C2 for Poison Ivy (2014) [S1]; compromised web servers and stolen VPN accounts as persistent access (2019) [S5]. Specific IOCs not captured.
diamond.victim: Uyghur-interest sites and sympathizers, US technology and academic organizations, a telecom provider (2014); government, managed service providers and multiple industries in about ten countries (2017-2019) [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage consistent with Chinese government interests per Fox-IT; the 2014 Uyghur focus indicates monitoring of a minority community [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing application servers such as JBoss, VPN gateways with software-token 2FA, password managers, and frequently visited websites [S1][S4].

gaps: WebFetch failed (host resolution errors) for all pages, so no primary document was opened. The Fox-IT Operation Wocao report, the Unit 42 th3bug report, MITRE C0014 and the Unit 42 Crawling Taurus page were read only through search-result excerpts.
Whether the 2014 th3bug cluster and the 2017-2019 Wocao cluster are the same operators rests on Fox-IT's medium-confidence TTP link and vendor naming; not independently verified.
Alias status of 'Twivy' and 'APT 8' appeared only in aggregator results (strobes.co, Malpedia excerpts) and was not confirmed in a vendor primary source, so not added.
No CrowdStrike VIOLIN PANDA report and no Mandiant APT20 profile were retrieved; the existing record's Mandiant and Unit 42 atoms URLs are unverified.
No public APT20 reporting after 2019 was found; current status of the actor is unknown.
Exact 2FA bypass method is unconfirmed; RSA SecurID token theft is Fox-IT's hypothesis [S5].
Specific malware families and indicators for Wocao were not retrieved.

Dark Reading and SecurityLab.ru sources were removed because their URLs could not be confirmed in search results; claims resting only on them (activity since 2009/2011, working-hours basis, construction and gambling targeting) were deleted.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing application servers (JBoss), VPN gateways, managed service provider access paths, and frequently visited community websites [S1][S4]. STEP 2: The actor reuses web servers already holding web shells and uses stolen VPN credentials as durable backdoors, which blurs initial access ownership and survives patching [S5]. STEP 3: Observed template is vulnerable web server or watering hole, then web shell or RAT, then credential theft, SMB lateral movement, VPN access and tool deletion [S1][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-duration collection against government, MSP and industry networks. MDCOA is use of a compromised MSP or stolen VPN/software token to reach defense-sector customers while bypassing 2FA. Candidate indicators: unexpected web shells on JBoss hosts, VPN logins from new locations that satisfy 2FA, token-generator files accessed on workstations, password-manager keylogging, SMB tool transfers and bulk deletion of tools [S4][S5]. Evidence is from 2014 and 2017-2019; current applicability is unverified.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track legacy JBoss and similar application servers and VPN authentication anomalies on mission networks. (2) Authorities: MSP and contractor compromise requires coordination with the owning organization and DIB reporting channels rather than direct action. (3) Mission assurance: treat software-token 2FA as bypassable if endpoint token seeds can be stolen, and prefer hardware-bound factors for privileged access. (4) Coordination: share indicators with the DIB cyber program and allied partners given the multinational victim set [S2][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: We’ve uncovered some new data and likely attribution regarding a series of APT watering hole attacks this past summer. Watering hole attacks are an increasingly popular component of APT campaigns, as many people are more aware of spear phishing and are less likely to open documents or click on links in unsolicited emails. Watering hole attacks offer a much better chance of success because they involve compromising legitimate websites and installing malware intended to compromise website visitors. These are often popular websites frequented by people who work in specific industries or have political sympathies to which the actors want to gain access. In contrast to many other APT campaigns, which tend to rely heavily on spear phishing to gain victims, “th3bug” is known for compromising legitimate websites their intended visitors are likely to frequent. Over the summer they compromised several sites, including a well-known Uyghur website written in that native language.
